Apostolic Succession
ap-oh-STOL-ik suk-SESH-un
noun phrase (a doctrine of ministerial lineage)
From “apostolic” and “succession” (Latin successio, a following after); the doctrine of an unbroken line of ordination and authority handed down from the apostles through the bishops.

Biblical Definition

Apostolic succession is the doctrine, held by Rome and the Eastern and Anglican churches, of an unbroken line of ordination and authority handed down by the laying on of hands from the apostles through an episcopal chain to the present clergy—so that valid ministry, and in the Roman view valid sacraments, depend on standing in that physical lineage. The dictionary distinguishes carefully. There is a true apostolic succession that Scripture commends: the succession of doctrine—the faithful handing-down of apostolic teaching from one generation to the next. Paul charges Timothy, “the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also”: a succession of truth, not of office-magic. The church is built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ Himself being the chief corner stone—a foundation laid once, not relaid in each generation. But the dictionary rejects the mechanical, tactile succession that grounds ministerial validity in an unbroken chain of episcopal hands rather than in fidelity to the apostolic gospel. Paul's own test of true ministry is doctrinal, not genealogical: though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel, let him be accursed. A church that holds the apostles' doctrine is apostolic, whatever its pedigree; a church that has departed from that doctrine is not apostolic though it can trace an unbroken line of hands. The dictionary holds that the Holy Ghost makes overseers and that the true succession is the succession of the faith once delivered—against the Roman use of tactile succession to deny the validity of Reformation churches and to bind the gospel to a lineage Christ never made the test.

Webster 1828 Definition

The doctrine of an unbroken episcopal line of ordination from the apostles, on which Rome grounds valid ministry and sacraments; the dictionary affirms the true succession of apostolic doctrine (2 Timothy 2:2) but rejects mechanical, tactile succession as the test.

APOSTOLIC SUCCESSION, noun phrase. An unbroken line of ordination handed down from the apostles through the bishops.

Rome grounds valid ministry and sacraments on standing in that lineage.

True succession is of doctrine: commit it to faithful men able to teach (2 Timothy 2:2).

The foundation of the apostles is laid once, in Christ the corner stone (Ephesians 2:20).

The test of apostolic ministry is the gospel, not genealogy (Galatians 1:8).

Key Scripture

Eph 2:20 — "And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;"

2 Ti 2:2 — "And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also."

Ac 20:28 — "Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood."

Ga 1:8 — "But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed."

Modern Corruption

The corruption is the mechanical, tactile succession that grounds ministerial validity in an unbroken chain of episcopal hands rather than fidelity to the apostolic gospel, used to unchurch Reformation congregations.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary distinguishes a true apostolic succession from a false one. The true succession, which Scripture commends, is the handing-down of apostolic doctrine: Paul charges Timothy to commit what he has heard to faithful men able to teach others—a succession of truth across the generations. The church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ the chief corner stone; that foundation is laid once and held by all who keep the apostles' teaching. A church faithful to the apostolic gospel is apostolic, whatever its pedigree.

The corruption is the mechanical, tactile succession that grounds the validity of ministry and sacraments in an unbroken physical chain of episcopal hands, apart from fidelity to the gospel—and uses that chain to unchurch the Reformation congregations and bind grace to a lineage. The dictionary rejects it. Paul's test of true ministry is doctrinal, not genealogical: though an angel from heaven preach another gospel, let him be accursed. The Holy Ghost makes overseers, and a church that has departed from the apostles' doctrine is not apostolic though it trace an unbroken line of hands. The succession that matters is the succession of the faith once delivered to the saints.

Hebrew Roots

From the Latin successio (a following after); the claimed unbroken chain of episcopal ordination, distinguished from the true succession of apostolic doctrine.

expand to see more

Successio, Latin, a following after, a succession.

The claimed unbroken chain of episcopal ordination by the laying on of hands.

True succession: the handing-down of apostolic doctrine (2 Timothy 2:2).

The apostolic foundation laid once in Christ (Ephesians 2:20).

The test of apostolicity: the gospel, not the genealogy of hands.

Usage

"The teacher affirmed the succession of apostolic doctrine while rejecting the tactile chain of hands."

"He held that a church faithful to the apostles' gospel is apostolic, whatever its pedigree."

"She answered that the Holy Ghost makes overseers, and the test of ministry is the gospel."
